claims.text: The target phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys inherently have limited glass-forming ability and marginal amorphous-state thermal stability.
Adding approximately 1 at% boron will enhance glass-forming ability in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
Adding approximately 1 at% boron will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
A boron addition will enhance local chemical disorder and atomic-size mismatch.
Atomic-radius mismatch disrupts the regular packing needed for crystalline phases and impedes crystal nucleation and growth.
Boron acts as a strong glass-forming element in the proposed alloys.
Boron introduces additional local heterogeneity and configurational entropy that disrupt regular atomic ordering.
The boron-induced structural changes will increase melt viscosity.
Increased melt viscosity impedes atomic diffusion and rearrangement required for crystal growth, thereby improving glass-forming ability.
Boron will elevate the activation-energy barrier for crystallization.
Crystallization of an amorphous alloy is kinetically controlled and occurs on heating when the relevant activation-energy barriers are overcome.
The boron-modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate than the otherwise comparable boron-free alloy.
The boron-modified alloy will have a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than the otherwise comparable boron-free alloy.
The beneficial effect should occur under rapid cooling and moderate annealing near the glass-transition and crystallization-onset temperatures.
Significantly higher boron concentrations or substantially different thermal processing may eliminate or reverse the benefit.
The effect of approximately 1 at% microalloying on glass formation depends on the identity and physical dissimilarity of the added element.
Boron microalloying has been shown in related systems to affect glass formation through changes in local atomic structure.
